description: Warning signs and red flag symptoms that require immediate medical attention

entries.title: Post-Menopausal Bleeding
entries.description: Any bleeding or spotting after menopause
entries.content: ANY bleeding or discharge after you've reached menopause (12 months without periods) is a red flag that requires immediate medical evaluation. This includes even light spotting or unusual discharge. Post-menopausal bleeding can be a sign of uterine (endometrial) cancer, though it can also have benign causes. It must always be investigated with ultrasound and possibly biopsy.
entries.why_serious: Can be a sign of uterine cancer
what_to_do: Do not wait or dismiss as normal
Expect ultrasound and possibly endometrial biopsy
entries.when_to_see_doctor: IMMEDIATELY - same day or next day

entries.title: Heavy or Prolonged Bleeding
entries.description: Very heavy periods or bleeding lasting more than 7 days
entries.content: Very heavy menstrual bleeding (soaking through pads/tampons hourly, passing large clots bigger than a quarter) or periods lasting longer than 7 days warrant medical evaluation. While often due to hormonal changes during perimenopause, heavy bleeding can lead to anemia and may indicate other conditions like fibroids, polyps, or rarely, cancer.
warning_signs: Passing blood clots larger than a quarter
Needing to change protection during night
why_concerning: May indicate fibroids, polyps, or other conditions
what_to_do: May need ultrasound or other testing
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Within days to a week; sooner if severe or causing dizziness/weakness

entries.title: Excessive Night Sweats with Weight Loss
entries.description: Soaking night sweats combined with unexplained weight loss
entries.content: While night sweats are common in menopause, soaking through sheets nightly combined with unexplained, unintentional weight loss is a red flag. This combination, especially with lumps in the armpit, neck, or groin, can indicate serious conditions like lymphoma. Normal menopausal night sweats do not cause significant weight loss.
red_flag_combination: Lumps in armpit, neck, or groin (lymph nodes)
entries.why_serious: Can indicate lymphoma or other serious conditions
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Within days if this combination of symptoms present

entries.title: Severe or New Pain
entries.description: Persistent, severe, or worsening pain in specific areas
entries.content: New or worsening severe pain, especially in the breast, pelvis, chest, or joints, requires medical evaluation. Pain that wakes you up at night, occurs without activity, or is progressively worsening is particularly concerning and may indicate serious conditions including cancer.
entries.urgency: prompt to immediate depending on severity and location
concerning_pain_characteristics: Pain that wakes you up at night
locations_of_concern: Breast pain (especially if localized, with lumps, or skin changes)
Pelvic pain (especially with bloating, feeling full quickly)
Back pain (especially with cough, weight loss, or breathing difficulty)
Joint pain (if severe, persistent, or with swelling)
entries.what_to_do: Contact doctor for evaluation; chest pain requires immediate attention
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Chest pain: IMMEDIATE (call emergency services). Other severe pain: within days

entries.title: Incontinence with Other Symptoms
entries.description: Urinary urgency/incontinence combined with bloating, pelvic pain, or feeling full
entries.content: While urinary incontinence is common during menopause (30-40% of women), the combination of incontinence with bloating, feeling full quickly when eating, pelvic pain, unintended weight loss, and changes in bowel habits can be a warning sign of ovarian cancer. Ovarian cancer symptoms are often vague and easily mistaken for menopause or digestive issues.
entries.why_serious: Can indicate ovarian cancer, which has vague early symptoms
what_to_do: Contact doctor if multiple symptoms present
Expect pelvic exam and possibly ultrasound
entries.important_note: Incontinence alone is common in menopause; it's the combination with other symptoms that's concerning
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Within 1-2 weeks if multiple symptoms present together

entries.title: Cognitive Changes Beyond Brain Fog
entries.description: Severe memory or cognitive problems suggesting dementia
entries.content: While brain fog and mild memory lapses are normal during menopause, more severe cognitive changes warrant evaluation for early-onset dementia or Alzheimer's disease. Warning signs include difficulty maintaining conversations, regularly forgetting where you are or what month/year it is, inability to manage finances or daily tasks, and personality changes noticed by family.
normal_menopause: Forgetting where you put keys occasionally
concerning_signs: Regularly forgetting month, year, or location
Can't remember how to do routine tasks (pay bills, cook familiar recipes)
entries.why_serious: May indicate early-onset Alzheimer's or dementia
what_to_do: Bring family member who can describe changes
Expect cognitive testing and possibly brain imaging
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Within weeks if severe cognitive changes present

entries.title: Fractures Before Menopause
entries.description: Broken bones before menopause indicating osteoporosis risk
entries.content: If you've broken bones, especially after age 50 but before menopause, you're at significantly greater risk for osteoporotic fractures after menopause. This is true even after accounting for other risk factors. Fractures before menopause warrant bone density testing and preventive measures.
entries.why_concerning: Indicates increased osteoporosis risk after menopause
what_to_do: Discuss preventive measures (calcium, vitamin D, exercise, possibly HRT)
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Discuss at next appointment; request bone density testing

entries.title: Symptoms with Thyroid or Autoimmune History
entries.description: Menopausal symptoms in women with thyroid problems or autoimmune diseases
entries.content: If you have an autoimmune disease (Type 1 diabetes, celiac disease) or family history of thyroid problems, and you're experiencing symptoms like weight gain, brain fog, fatigue, temperature regulation issues, and irregular periods, it's important to rule out hypothyroidism (especially Hashimoto's disease). These symptoms overlap significantly with menopause but require different treatment.
risk_factors: Personal history of autoimmune disease (Type 1 diabetes, celiac disease)
entries.why_important: Hypothyroidism requires different treatment than menopause
what_to_do: May need thyroid treatment in addition to or instead of menopause treatment

entries.title: History of Major Depression
entries.description: Previous major depressive episodes increase perimenopause depression risk
entries.content: If you've had a major depressive episode in the past, you are 59% more likely to experience another episode during perimenopause. Fluctuating estrogen can trigger depression, and it's important to recognize symptoms early and seek help. Don't dismiss persistent sadness, hopelessness, or loss of interest as 'just menopause.'
entries.risk_factor: History of major depressive episode increases perimenopause depression risk by 59%
warning_signs: Loss of interest in activities you used to enjoy
entries.why_important: Depression requires treatment; don't dismiss as normal menopause
what_to_do: Recognize that you're at higher risk
Seek help early if depression symptoms develop
Treatment may include therapy, antidepressants, and/or HRT
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Promptly if depression symptoms develop; immediately if thoughts of self-harm

entries.title: Doctor Dismisses Your Concerns
entries.description: Healthcare provider not taking your symptoms seriously
entries.content: If your doctor dismisses your menopause concerns, doesn't listen to your symptoms, refuses to discuss treatment options, or makes you feel like you're overreacting, it's a red flag that you need a new healthcare provider. You deserve a doctor who takes your symptoms seriously, discusses treatment options, and partners with you in managing your menopause transition.
signs_of_dismissive_care: Doctor says symptoms are 'just part of aging' without offering help
Refuses to discuss HRT or other treatments
Makes you feel like you're overreacting
Won't answer questions or provide information
entries.why_important: You deserve quality care and symptom management
what_to_do: Find a new doctor or gynecologist
Look for providers with menopause expertise
your_rights: To ask questions and get answers
entries.when_to_see_doctor: Find a new provider if current one is dismissive
